newsitem.title: UK: Albright, Rifkind want smooth China power switch.
newsitem.headline: Albright, Rifkind want smooth China power switch.

text.p: The United States and Britain paid tribute on Wednesday to China's late paramount leader Deng Xiaoping as a historic figure and expressed the hope for a quick and tidy handover of power in Beijing.
"It would obviously be a great advantage to the Chinese as well as to all of us if there were a smooth transition," visiting U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright told reporters.
Albright said it was too early to say what impact Deng's death would have on U.S.-Chinese ties but stressed that Washington wanted to pursue a "multi-faceted and important relationship" with Beijing.
Albright, on her maiden overseas trip as secretary of state, heard of Deng's death during talks with British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind.

Rifkind called Deng, who died aged 93 of complications from Parkinson's disease and a lung infection, a very major historic figure who could take credit for opening up China and driving through massive economic reforms.

"But because of the state of his health he has been unable clearly to provide momentum over the last few years, and therefore there has been a hiatus -- particularly with regard to political change and further economic reform.

"We would assume that there will now be a period -- we hope a short period -- of uncertainty as a new leadership emerges. But once that is consolidated, then we very much hope that the economic and political reforms will gather speed," Rifkind said.

Albright, who plans to consult with Chinese officials whether to continue with a planned stopover in Beijing next week, said the United States would particularly remember Deng for the important part he played in normalising Sino-American relations.
But history's overall assessment would be mixed.
The Tiananmen Square killings in June 1989 were "very troublesome to everybody that has been following the issue of human rights in China," Albright said.
"But I think also one does have to see him as a historic figure who did in fact open China up... It is a mixed assessment," she added.

Rifkind said he hoped the transition to a new leader would be troublefree not just because of the importance of China itself but also because of Britain's responsibility for Hong Kong, which it will hand back to China at midnight on June 30.

"The more that China itself reforms -- the more it becomes an open society and a market economy -- the more confidence we'll be able to have that Hong Kong's own special identity will be respected and the freedom of its people will be safeguarded," Rifkind said.

Earlier, Prime Minister John Major said it was Deng's "visionary concept of one country, two systems'" that had facilitated the 1984 declaration between Britain and China, guaranteeing Hong Kong's capitalist system would stay in place for 50 years after the British colony is handed back.
